quizzes.title: 24.1 Module 24 Introduction: The Iron Curtain
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRODUCTION
Module Introduction: The Iron Curtain
Survey · 2 questions · not graded
║ ─ ║ ─ ║
Before you start

Welcome to The Iron Curtain. Answer the questions below before you open the first lesson. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting. This survey is not graded.

This module's goals:
  • Describe the agreements at Yalta and Potsdam and how the Soviet Union came to control Eastern Europe.
  • Explain containment, the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, and the Berlin Blockade.
  • Describe the founding of NATO and the Warsaw Pact and weigh who divided Europe.

questions.text: Before you read: Who divided Europe? Give your first answer in two or three sentences. You will answer it again at the end of the module, so it is fine if your answer changes.
I have read this module's goals and I know what I am working toward this week.

answers.text: Yes, I have read them
Not yet, I will read them before the first lesson

quizzes.title: 24.7 Reading Quiz: The Iron Curtain
quizzes.description:
READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: The Iron Curtain
7 questions · 7 points
║ ─ ║ ─ ║
Before you start

This quiz covers both lessons and both primary sources for this module. It has 7 questions. Most ask you to work something out from what you read, not to find a sentence in the text. You may look back at the lessons and sources while you work.

HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and keep your notes in My Notebook. Then answer the questions below.

questions.text: At Yalta the Western leaders won a promise of free elections in Poland. Critics say Roosevelt gave Eastern Europe away, and defenders say he gave nothing. What do both sides agree on, and what does the defenders’ case rest on?

answers.text: The promise was kept, and the defenders say Stalin broke it later
The promise of free elections was not kept, and the defenders say the Red Army already held the ground, so the West held only a promise
The Western armies held Eastern Europe, so Roosevelt could have enforced the promise
Roosevelt did not discuss Poland at Yalta, so the promise was never made

questions.text: Kennan wrote that Soviet power “is highly sensitive to logic of force” and “can easily withdraw” when it meets strong resistance. Which policy follows from that view?

answers.text: Give way on small points so that the Soviets feel secure
Attack the Soviet Union at once while the United States held the atomic bomb
Leave Europe to the Soviets and keep out of its quarrels
Resist each Soviet advance firmly and patiently, without trying to roll back Soviet power by force

questions.text: Truman asked Congress for money for Greece and Turkey, but his address never names the Soviet Union and speaks of “free peoples” everywhere. What does this show about the speech?

answers.text: It set a general policy of supporting free peoples who resist pressure, and Greece and Turkey were only the occasion
It shows that Greece and Turkey were the only countries in danger
It shows that Truman believed the Soviet Union was not a danger
It shows that Congress had asked him not to name any country

questions.text: The Marshall Plan invited every European nation, including the Soviet Union. Why did Stalin refuse and force Czechoslovakia to take back its acceptance?

answers.text: He believed Europe could recover without any help
He had not been told that the offer included the East
He feared the aid would draw his satellites toward the West, so he put his control of them ahead of their recovery
The aid could be used only by countries that already belonged to NATO

questions.text: The blockade of Berlin was meant to stop a West German state. What did it actually do?

answers.text: It made the Western powers give up their zones of Berlin
It drove West Germans and the Western powers closer together and showed the Soviets as bullies to a watching world
It brought the Soviet Union and the United States into open war
It ended the plan for a new currency in West Germany

questions.text: NATO’s Article 5 said an armed attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all. Why does the lesson say this was a break with the past?

answers.text: It was the first peacetime alliance with European powers the United States had joined since 1778, against the old advice to avoid such entanglements
It was the first time the United States had ever signed a treaty
It was the first alliance that included the Soviet Union
It made the United Nations unnecessary

questions.text: A student argues that Europe was divided by where the armies stood in 1945, whatever Stalin or Truman chose afterward. Which evidence from the lessons best supports this view?

answers.text: Czechoslovakia accepted the Marshall Plan invitation
Yugoslavia broke from Moscow in 1948
The Americans and British merged their zones in 1947
The Red Army held Eastern Europe at the end of the war, and Western leaders held only a promise of free elections

discussions.title: 24.8 Discussion: Who divided Europe?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Who divided Europe?
Stalin, the West, or the positions of the armies in 1945?
Graded discussion · 10 points · one post and one reply
║ ─ ║ ─ ║
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then post your answer to the prompt below, and reply to one classmate.
DISCUSSION PROMPT

This week’s question: Who divided Europe?

Choose one answer: Stalin and the Soviet Union, the Western powers, or the positions of the armies in 1945. Use your three-column chart. Name two decisions, with their dates and who made them, that support your answer. Then name one different choice that could have led to a different Europe, and say what might have followed.

Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Then add one sentence on responsibility. What did the great powers owe the peoples of the lands where their armies stood? Say what you think and why.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a fact or decision they did not use. If not, say politely where you think it falls short, and give your reason.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
CriteriaSubstantive (full credit)Thin (partial credit)Missing (no credit)
Your claim and your reasons
6 pts		Takes a clear side, uses the specific evidence the prompt asks for, and explains why it supports the claim.Takes a side but gives general reasons, or leaves out part of what the prompt asks for.No post, or no claim.
Your reply to a classmate
4 pts		Answers one classmate's actual reasoning. Strengthens it or says where it falls short, politely and with a reason.Replies, but only to agree or disagree with no reason.No reply.
10 pts total
